title: Discrete entropy: how many bits of uncertainty?
subtitle: Change a probability distribution and watch H = −Σ p<sub>i</sub> log<sub>2</sub> p<sub>i</sub> respond.

intro.idea: A random source picks one of n outcomes with probabilities p1, …, pn. Its entropy H measures how uncertain we are about which outcome will occur, i.e. the average “surprise” per outcome. Measured with base-2 logarithms, H is in bits.
intro.why: Entropy is the yardstick of information theory: it is the minimum average number of bits per symbol needed to encode the source without loss, so it sets the limit for compression and tells an engineer how much information a channel must carry.
steps: Each outcome i has probability p<sub>i</sub> ≥ 0, and all probabilities sum to 1.
Its surprise is −log<sub>2</sub> p<sub>i</sub>: rare outcomes are very surprising, a sure outcome (p<sub>i</sub> = 1) has zero surprise.
Its contribution to the average is p<sub>i</sub> × (−log<sub>2</sub> p<sub>i</sub>). Outcomes with p<sub>i</sub> = 0 contribute 0.
H is the sum of the contributions. It is 0 for a certain outcome and at most log<sub>2</sub> n, reached when all n outcomes are equally likely.

symbols.meaning: positive constant in Shannon's formula; it only chooses the unit (base-2 logs give bits)

controls.label: Weights (normalized to probabilities)
controls.help: Type any non-negative weights; the page divides by their sum to get p<sub>i</sub>. Press Normalize to rewrite them as probabilities.

visuals.title: Probabilities and their contributions to H
visuals.caption: Blue: probability of each outcome. Orange: how many bits that outcome adds to H. A bar of height 1 in blue gives an orange bar of 0.

visuals.title: H never exceeds log<sub>2</sub> n
visuals.caption: The curve is the upper bound log<sub>2</sub> n. The red dot is your distribution. It touches the curve only when all outcomes are equally likely.

explorations.title: Certainty vs. four equally likely outcomes
explorations.change: Press Try it (one outcome has probability 1). Then set all four weights to 1.
explorations.observe: With a certain outcome H = 0 bits. With four equal outcomes H = 2 bits, exactly log<sub>2</sub> 4, and the red dot sits on the curve.
explorations.why: A sure outcome carries no surprise (−log<sub>2</sub> 1 = 0). With four equally likely outcomes each one has surprise log<sub>2</sub> 4 = 2 bits, and that is the largest average possible for n = 4.

explorations.title: Impossible outcomes, and what entropy does not measure
explorations.change: Press Try it: two outcomes at 0.5 and two at 0. Then increase n to 8 (new outcomes get weight 0), and finally swap the order of the weights.
explorations.observe: H stays at 1 bit even though log<sub>2</sub> n grows. Reordering the weights also leaves H unchanged.
explorations.why: By convention 0 · log 0 = 0 (the limit of p log p as p → 0), so impossible outcomes add nothing; they are not an error. Entropy depends only on the probability values, not on which outcome has which value or what the outcomes mean. It measures uncertainty, not the meaning or usefulness of a message.

limitations: Outcomes are treated as independent draws from a fixed, known distribution. Shannon's later sections handle sources with memory, which this demo does not cover.
Zero probabilities use the convention 0 · log<sub>2</sub> 0 = 0. Typing all-zero weights does not define a distribution, so H is undefined (the page warns you).
Entropy measures uncertainty about which outcome occurs, not the meaning, value or importance of the outcomes.
Base-2 logarithms give bits. Shannon's constant K only fixes the unit; natural logs would give the same idea in nats.

tests.name: Four equally likely outcomes give 2 bits
Eight equally likely outcomes give 3 bits
Default distribution (½, ¼, ⅛, ⅛) gives 1.75 bits

source.section: Part I, Section 6: Choice, Uncertainty and Entropy
source.equation: H = −K Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> p<sub>i</sub> log p<sub>i</sub>   (Theorem 2, with K = 1 and base-2 logs here)

supported.claim: Entropy has the form H = −Σ p<sub>i</sub> log p<sub>i</sub>, and K only sets the unit.
supported.quote: the constant K merely amounts to a choice of a unit of measure

supported.claim: H is zero only when the outcome is certain.
supported.quote: H = 0 if and only if all the pi but one are zero, this one having the value unity

supported.claim: For a given n, H is largest, log n, when all outcomes are equally likely.
supported.quote: For a given n, H is a maximum and equal to log n when all the pi are equal

simplifications: We fix K = 1 and use base-2 logarithms so H is in bits.
We limit n to 8 outcomes and let you type unnormalized weights that are divided by their sum.
The step-by-step table, the presets and the specific example distributions are our own illustrations, not from the paper.
